items.stem: Prove that : (1 + sec A)/sec A = sin²A/(1 + cos A)
items.answer: LHS = (1 + sec A)/sec A = (1 + 1/cos A) ÷ (1/cos A) = (cos A + 1)/1 = 1 + cos A. RHS = sin²A/(1 − cos A) = (1 − cos²A)/(1 − cos A) = (1 + cos A)(1 − cos A)/(1 − cos A) = 1 + cos A. Since both sides reduce to 1 + cos A, LHS = RHS, hence proved.
items.section_heading: THREE MARKS QUESTIONS | Board 2023 OD Standard
items.ocr: Stem/solution conflict: the question line prints the right side as sin²A/(1 + cos A), but the worked solution takes RHS = sin²A/(1 − cos A) throughout, which is the identity that is actually true (LHS = 1 + cos A). Solution wins; the stem is kept as printed.

items.stem: Show that : [cos²(45° + θ) + cos²(45° − θ)] / [tan(60° + θ) tan(30° − θ)] = 1
items.answer: Use complementary angles. cos(45° − θ) = sin(90° − 45° + θ) = sin(45° + θ), so the numerator becomes cos²(45° + θ) + sin²(45° + θ) = 1. Also tan(30° − θ) = cot(90° − 30° + θ) = cot(60° + θ), so the denominator becomes tan(60° + θ)·cot(60° + θ) = 1. Hence LHS = 1/1 = 1 = RHS.
items.section_heading: THREE MARKS QUESTIONS | Board 2020 OD Standard

items.stem: The rod of TV disc antenna is fixed at right angles to wall AB and a rod CD is supporting the disc as shown in Figure. If AC = 1.5 m long and CD = 3 m, find (i) tan θ (ii) sec θ + cosec θ.
items.answer: In right triangle CAD, right angled at A, Pythagoras gives AD² + AC² = DC², so AD² = 3² − (1.5)² = 9 − 2.25 = 6.75 and AD = √6.75 ≈ 2.6 m. (i) tan θ = AC/AD = 1.5/2.6 = 15/26. (ii) sec θ = CD/AD = 3/2.6 = 15/13 and cosec θ = CD/AC = 3/1.5 = 2, so sec θ + cosec θ = 15/13 + 26/13 = 41/13.

items.stem: Prove that : (cot θ + cosec θ − 1)/(cot θ − cosec θ + 1) = (1 + cos θ)/sin θ
items.answer: Write cot θ = cos θ/sin θ and cosec θ = 1/sin θ. LHS = (cos θ + 1 − sin θ)/(cos θ − 1 + sin θ) after clearing sin θ from numerator and denominator. Multiply numerator and denominator by sin θ: numerator becomes sin θ cos θ + sin θ − sin²θ = sin θ cos θ + sin θ − (1 − cos²θ) = sin θ(cos θ + 1) − (1 − cos θ)(1 + cos θ) = (1 + cos θ)(sin θ − 1 + cos θ). Denominator becomes sin θ(cos θ + sin θ − 1). Cancelling the common factor (sin θ + cos θ − 1) leaves (1 + cos θ)/sin θ = RHS.
items.section_heading: THREE MARKS QUESTIONS | Board 2020 Delhi Standard

items.stem: If sin θ + cos θ = √2 prove that tan θ + cot θ = 2
items.answer: Squaring sin θ + cos θ = √2 gives sin²θ + cos²θ + 2 sin θ cos θ = 2, so 1 + 2 sin θ cos θ = 2 and sin θ cos θ = ½. Now tan θ + cot θ = sin θ/cos θ + cos θ/sin θ = (sin²θ + cos²θ)/(sin θ cos θ) = 1/(sin θ cos θ) = 1 ÷ ½ = 2. Hence proved.
items.section_heading: THREE MARKS QUESTIONS | Board 2020 OD Standard, SQP 2018

items.stem: If 1 + sin²θ = 3 sin θ cos θ, prove that tan θ = 1 or ½.
items.answer: Divide both sides by sin²θ: 1/sin²θ + 1 = 3 cos θ/sin θ, i.e. cosec²θ + 1 = 3 cot θ. Using cosec²θ = 1 + cot²θ this becomes cot²θ + 2 = 3 cot θ, i.e. cot²θ − 3 cot θ + 2 = 0. Factorising, (cot θ − 2)(cot θ − 1) = 0, so cot θ = 2 or 1. Taking reciprocals, tan θ = ½ or 1. Hence proved.
items.section_heading: THREE MARKS QUESTIONS | Board 2020 OD Standard

items.stem: Prove that (sin θ + cosec θ)² + (cos θ + sec θ)² = 7 + tan²θ + cot²θ
items.answer: Expanding, LHS = (sin²θ + cosec²θ + 2 sin θ cosec θ) + (cos²θ + sec²θ + 2 cos θ sec θ) = (sin²θ + cos²θ) + (cosec²θ + sec²θ) + 2 sin θ·(1/sin θ) + 2 cos θ·(1/cos θ) = 1 + (1 + cot²θ) + (1 + tan²θ) + 2 + 2 = 7 + tan²θ + cot²θ = RHS.
items.section_heading: THREE MARKS QUESTIONS | Board 2019 Delhi Standard

items.stem: Prove that (1 + cot A − cosec A)(1 + tan A + sec A) = 2
items.answer: LHS = (1 + cos A/sin A − 1/sin A)(1 + sin A/cos A + 1/cos A) = [(sin A + cos A − 1)/sin A]·[(cos A + sin A + 1)/cos A] = [(sin A + cos A)² − 1²]/(sin A cos A) = (sin²A + cos²A + 2 sin A cos A − 1)/(sin A cos A) = (1 + 2 sin A cos A − 1)/(sin A cos A) = 2 sin A cos A/(sin A cos A) = 2 = RHS.

items.stem: Prove that (sin A − cos A − 1)/(sin A + cos A − 1) = 1/(sec A − tan A)
items.answer: Take LHS = (sin A − cos A + 1)/(sin A + cos A − 1) and multiply numerator and denominator by (1 + sin A). The denominator becomes sin A + cos A − 1 + sin²A + cos A sin A − sin A = −1 + cos A + (1 − cos²A) + sin A cos A = cos A(1 − cos A + sin A). The numerator is (sin A − cos A + 1)(1 + sin A). Cancelling (1 − cos A + sin A) leaves (1 + sin A)/cos A = sec A + tan A. Finally sec A + tan A = (sec A + tan A)(sec A − tan A)/(sec A − tan A) = (sec²A − tan²A)/(sec A − tan A) = 1/(sec A − tan A) = RHS.
items.ocr: Stem/solution conflict: the question line prints the numerator as sin A − cos A − 1, but the worked solution starts from LHS = (sin A − cos A + 1)/(sin A + cos A − 1), which is the identity that actually holds. Solution wins; the stem is kept as printed.

items.stem: Prove that : 2(sin⁶θ + cos⁶θ) − 3(sin⁴θ + cos⁴θ) + 1 = 0
items.answer: Write sin⁶θ + cos⁶θ = (sin²θ)³ + (cos²θ)³ = (sin²θ + cos²θ)(sin⁴θ − sin²θ cos²θ + cos⁴θ) = sin⁴θ − sin²θ cos²θ + cos⁴θ. So LHS = 2(sin⁴θ + cos⁴θ − sin²θ cos²θ) − 3(sin⁴θ + cos⁴θ) + 1 = −(sin⁴θ + cos⁴θ) − 2 sin²θ cos²θ + 1 = −(sin⁴θ + cos⁴θ + 2 sin²θ cos²θ) + 1 = −(sin²θ + cos²θ)² + 1 = −1 + 1 = 0. Hence proved.
items.section_heading: THREE MARKS QUESTIONS | Board 2020 Delhi Standard

items.stem: Prove that tan²A/(tan²A − 1) + cosec²A/(sec²A − cosec²A) = 1/(1 − 2cos²A)
items.answer: Write everything in sin A and cos A. The first term = (sin²A/cos²A) ÷ [(sin²A − cos²A)/cos²A] = sin²A/(sin²A − cos²A). The second term = (1/sin²A) ÷ [(sin²A − cos²A)/(cos²A sin²A)] = cos²A/(sin²A − cos²A). Adding, LHS = (sin²A + cos²A)/(sin²A − cos²A) = 1/(sin²A − cos²A) = 1/[(1 − cos²A) − cos²A] = 1/(1 − 2cos²A) = RHS.

items.stem: If in a triangle ABC right angled at B, AB = 6 units and BC = 8 units, then find the value of sin A cos C + cos A sin C.
items.answer: By Pythagoras, AC² = 8² + 6² = 100, so AC = 10 units. Then sin A = BC/AC = 8/10, cos A = AB/AC = 6/10, sin C = AB/AC = 6/10 and cos C = BC/AC = 8/10. Hence sin A cos C + cos A sin C = (8/10)(8/10) + (6/10)(6/10) = 64/100 + 36/100 = 100/100 = 1.
items.ocr: The triangle drawn on the page is a solution figure ("As per question statement figure is shown below") and was not attached. The solution writes AC = 10 cm though the question gives lengths in units.

items.stem: Evaluate : (5cos²60° + 4cos²30° − tan²45°)/(sin²30° + cos²60°)
items.answer: Substituting cos 60° = ½, cos 30° = √3/2, tan 45° = 1 and sin 30° = ½: numerator = 5(½)² + 4(√3/2)² − 1² = 5/4 + 3 − 1 = 5/4 + 2 = 13/4; denominator = (½)² + (½)² = ¼ + ¼ = ½. Hence the value is (13/4) ÷ (1/2) = 13/2.
items.section_heading: THREE MARKS QUESTIONS | Board Term-1 OD 2013

items.stem: If cos(40° + x) = sin 30°, find the value of x.
items.answer: Write the right side as a cosine: sin 30° = sin(90° − 60°) = cos 60°. So cos(40° + x) = cos 60°, giving 40° + x = 60°. Hence x = 60° − 40° = 20°.
items.ocr: The first line of the printed solution misprints the equation as cos(40° − x) = sin 30°; every later line uses cos(40° + x) as in the stem, and the answer x = 20° follows from the stem.

items.stem: In the given ∠PQR, right-angled at Q, QR = 9 cm and PR − PQ = 1 cm. Determine the value of sin R + cos R.
items.answer: Let PQ = x, so PR = x + 1. By Pythagoras, PQ² + QR² = PR², i.e. x² + 9² = (x + 1)², so x² + 81 = x² + 2x + 1, giving 2x = 80 and PQ = 40 cm. Then PR = 41 cm. Now sin R = PQ/PR = 40/41 and cos R = QR/PR = 9/41, so sin R + cos R = 40/41 + 9/41 = 49/41.
items.ocr: The book prints "∠PQR" where triangle PQR is meant. The labelled right triangle printed between the stem and the solution is the question figure and was cropped; the printed working writes PQ = 40 directly after PQ² + 81 = PQ² + 1 + 2PQ.

items.stem: If tan A + cot A = 2, then find the value of tan²A + cot²A.
items.answer: Squaring both sides, (tan A + cot A)² = 2², so tan²A + cot²A + 2 tan A cot A = 4. Since cot A = 1/tan A, the middle term is 2 tan A × (1/tan A) = 2. Hence tan²A + cot²A + 2 = 4, giving tan²A + cot²A = 2.

items.stem: If cos θ + sin θ = √2 cos θ, show that cos θ − sin θ = √2 cos θ.
items.answer: From cos θ + sin θ = √2 cos θ we get sin θ = (√2 − 1) cos θ. Rationalising, sin θ = [(√2 − 1)(√2 + 1)/(√2 + 1)] cos θ = cos θ/(√2 + 1). Hence (√2 + 1) sin θ = cos θ, i.e. √2 sin θ + sin θ = cos θ, which rearranges to cos θ − sin θ = √2 sin θ. Hence proved.
items.ocr: Stem/solution conflict: the question asks to show cos θ − sin θ = √2 cos θ, but the worked solution ends at cos θ − sin θ = √2 sin θ, which is the correct consequence. Solution wins; the stem is kept as printed.

items.stem: Prove that : cos A/(1 − tan A) + sin A/(1 − cot A) = sin A + cos A.
items.answer: LHS = cos A/[1 − (sin A/cos A)] + sin A/[1 − (cos A/sin A)] = cos²A/(cos A − sin A) + sin²A/(sin A − cos A) = cos²A/(cos A − sin A) − sin²A/(cos A − sin A) = (cos²A − sin²A)/(cos A − sin A) = (cos A − sin A)(cos A + sin A)/(cos A − sin A) = cos A + sin A = sin A + cos A = RHS.

items.stem: In Δ ABC, ∠B = 90°, BC = 5 cm, AC − AB = 1, Evaluate : (1 + sin C)/(1 + cos C).
items.answer: Let AB = x, so AC = x + 1. By Pythagoras AC² = AB² + BC², i.e. (x + 1)² = x² + 5², giving x² + 2x + 1 = x² + 25, so 2x = 24 and x = 12. Hence AB = 12 cm and AC = 13 cm. Then sin C = AB/AC = 12/13 and cos C = BC/AC = 5/13, so (1 + sin C)/(1 + cos C) = (1 + 12/13)/(1 + 5/13) = (25/13)/(18/13) = 25/18.
items.ocr: The triangle on the page is drawn inside the solution ("As per question we have drawn the figure given below") and was not attached.

items.stem: Prove that : cos A/(1 + tan A) − sin A/(1 + cot A) = cos A − sin A
items.answer: LHS = cos A/[1 + (sin A/cos A)] − sin A/[1 + (cos A/sin A)] = cos²A/(cos A + sin A) − sin²A/(sin A + cos A) = (cos²A − sin²A)/(sin A + cos A) = (cos A + sin A)(cos A − sin A)/(sin A + cos A) = cos A − sin A = RHS.

items.stem: If b cos θ = a, then prove that cosec θ + cot θ = √[(b + a)/(b − a)].
items.answer: From b cos θ = a we get cos θ = a/b, so in a right triangle with angle θ the adjacent side is a and the hypotenuse is b, and the opposite side is √(b² − a²). Hence cosec θ = b/√(b² − a²) and cot θ = a/√(b² − a²). Adding, cosec θ + cot θ = (b + a)/√(b² − a²) = (b + a)/√[(b + a)(b − a)] = √[(b + a)/(b − a)]. Hence proved.
items.ocr: The labelled triangle on the page belongs to the solution ("Now consider the triangle shown below") and was not attached.

items.stem: Prove that : (sin θ − 2 sin³θ)/(2 cos³ − cos θ) = tan θ
items.answer: Factor each side: numerator = sin θ(1 − 2 sin²θ) and denominator = cos θ(2 cos²θ − 1). Using sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, 1 − 2 sin²θ = (sin²θ + cos²θ) − 2 sin²θ = cos²θ − sin²θ, and 2 cos²θ − 1 = 2 cos²θ − (sin²θ + cos²θ) = cos²θ − sin²θ. So the expression = sin θ(cos²θ − sin²θ)/[cos θ(cos²θ − sin²θ)] = sin θ/cos θ = tan θ. Hence proved.
items.ocr: The denominator is printed as 2 cos³ − cos θ with the θ missing from the cubed term; the solution treats it as 2 cos³θ − cos θ. The board tag is misprinted "Bard Term-1 2015" and has been normalised to Board Term-1 2015.

items.stem: When is an equation called 'an identity'. Prove the trigonometric identity 1 + tan²A = sec²A.
items.answer: An equation is called an identity when it is true for every admissible value of the variable in it; on simplifying an identity one always arrives at a true statement. For the proof take a right triangle with perpendicular P, base B and hypotenuse H for the angle A, so tan A = P/B, sec A = H/B and H² = P² + B². Then 1 + tan²A = 1 + (P/B)² = (B² + P²)/B² = H²/B² = (H/B)² = sec²A. Hence 1 + tan²A = sec²A.
items.ocr: The question begins on page 19 and its solution, including the labelled P-B-H triangle, runs onto page 20; that triangle is a solution figure and was not attached.

items.stem: Prove that : (cot θ − cosec θ)² = (1 − cos θ)/(1 + cos θ)
items.answer: cot θ − cosec θ = cos θ/sin θ − 1/sin θ = (cos θ − 1)/sin θ. Squaring, (cot θ − cosec θ)² = (cos θ − 1)²/sin²θ = (1 − cos θ)²/(1 − cos²θ) = (1 − cos θ)(1 − cos θ)/[(1 − cos θ)(1 + cos θ)] = (1 − cos θ)/(1 + cos θ). Hence proved.

items.stem: Prove that : (cosec θ − sin θ)(sec θ − cos θ)(tan θ + cot θ) = 1
items.answer: LHS = (1/sin θ − sin θ)(1/cos θ − cos θ)(sin θ/cos θ + cos θ/sin θ) = [(1 − sin²θ)/sin θ]·[(1 − cos²θ)/cos θ]·[(sin²θ + cos²θ)/(sin θ cos θ)] = (cos²θ/sin θ)·(sin²θ/cos θ)·[1/(sin θ cos θ)] = (cos θ sin θ)·[1/(sin θ cos θ)] = 1 = RHS.
items.ocr: The solution's last step runs over to the top of page 21 (= cos θ sin θ × 1/(sin θ cos θ) = 1).

items.stem: Prove that : cosec²θ/(cosec θ − 1) − cosec²θ/(cosec θ + 1) = 2 sec²θ
items.answer: LHS = cosec²θ[1/(1/sin θ − 1) − 1/(1/sin θ + 1)] = cosec²θ[sin θ/(1 − sin θ) − sin θ/(1 + sin θ)] = (1/sin²θ)·sin θ·[(1 + sin θ) − (1 − sin θ)]/[(1 − sin θ)(1 + sin θ)] = (1/sin θ)·[2 sin θ/(1 − sin²θ)] = 2/cos²θ = 2 sec²θ = RHS.

items.stem: Prove that : 1/(cosec A − cot A) − 1/sin A = 1/sin A − 1/(cosec A + cot A).
items.answer: Rearrange the statement as 1/(cosec A − cot A) + 1/(cosec A + cot A) = 1/sin A + 1/sin A = 2/sin A. Adding the two fractions on the left gives [(cosec A + cot A) + (cosec A − cot A)]/[(cosec A − cot A)(cosec A + cot A)] = 2 cosec A/(cosec²A − cot²A). Since cosec²A − cot²A = 1, this is 2 cosec A = 2/sin A, which equals the right side. Hence proved.
items.ocr: One line of the printed working mistypes cot A as cot a inside (cosec A + cot a); it is cot A.

items.stem: If sec θ = x + 1/(4x) prove that sec θ + tan θ = 2x or, 1/(2x)
items.answer: Square the given relation: sec²θ = x² + 2·x·1/(4x) + 1/(16x²) = x² + ½ + 1/(16x²). Since sec²θ = 1 + tan²θ, tan²θ = x² + ½ + 1/(16x²) − 1 = x² − ½ + 1/(16x²) = (x − 1/(4x))². Taking square roots, tan θ = ±(x − 1/(4x)). Adding sec θ = x + 1/(4x) to tan θ = x − 1/(4x) gives sec θ + tan θ = 2x; adding it instead to tan θ = −x + 1/(4x) gives sec θ + tan θ = 1/(4x) + 1/(4x) = 1/(2x). Hence sec θ + tan θ = 2x or 1/(2x).
items.ocr: The question begins on page 20 and its solution continues on page 21.

items.stem: Prove that : (sin θ − cos θ)/(sin θ + cos θ) + (sin θ + cos θ)/(sin θ − cos θ) = 2/(2 sin²θ − 1)
items.answer: Taking the common denominator, LHS = [(sin θ − cos θ)² + (sin θ + cos θ)²]/(sin²θ − cos²θ). The numerator is (sin²θ + cos²θ − 2 sin θ cos θ) + (sin²θ + cos²θ + 2 sin θ cos θ) = 1 + 1 = 2. The denominator is sin²θ − (1 − sin²θ) = 2 sin²θ − 1. Hence LHS = 2/(2 sin²θ − 1) = RHS.

items.stem: If x sin³θ + y cos³θ = sin θ cos θ and x sin θ = y cos θ, prove that x² + y² = 1.
items.answer: From x sin θ = y cos θ we get x = y cos θ/sin θ. Substituting into the first relation, (y cos θ/sin θ) sin³θ + y cos³θ = sin θ cos θ, i.e. y cos θ sin²θ + y cos³θ = sin θ cos θ, so y cos θ(sin²θ + cos²θ) = sin θ cos θ, giving y(sin²θ + cos²θ) = sin θ and therefore y = sin θ. Putting this back, x = sin θ·cos θ/sin θ = cos θ. Squaring and adding, x² + y² = cos²θ + sin²θ = 1. Hence proved.

items.stem: Prove that (cos³θ + sin³θ)/(cos θ + sin θ) + (cos³θ − sin³θ)/(cos θ − sin θ) = 2
items.answer: Using a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²), the first term = (cos θ + sin θ)(cos²θ + sin²θ − sin θ cos θ)/(cos θ + sin θ) = 1 − sin θ cos θ. Using a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²), the second term = (cos θ − sin θ)(cos²θ + sin²θ + sin θ cos θ)/(cos θ − sin θ) = 1 + sin θ cos θ. Adding, the sum = (1 − sin θ cos θ) + (1 + sin θ cos θ) = 2 = RHS.

items.stem: Express : sin A, tan A and cosec A in terms of sec A.
items.answer: From sin²A + cos²A = 1, sin A = √(1 − cos²A) = √(1 − 1/sec²A) = √[(sec²A − 1)/sec²A] = √(sec²A − 1)/sec A. Next tan A = sin A/cos A = sin A · sec A = [√(sec²A − 1)/sec A]·sec A = √(sec²A − 1). Finally cosec A = 1/sin A = sec A/√(sec²A − 1). So sin A = √(sec²A − 1)/sec A, tan A = √(sec²A − 1) and cosec A = sec A/√(sec²A − 1).

items.stem: Show that : [cos²(45° + θ) + cos²(45° − θ)] / [tan(60° + θ) tan(30° − θ)] = 1
items.answer: Convert one term of each pair with complementary angles. cos(45° − θ) = sin(90° − 45° + θ) = sin(45° + θ), so the numerator = cos²(45° + θ) + sin²(45° + θ) = 1. Also tan(30° − θ) = cot(90° − 30° + θ) = cot(60° + θ), so the denominator = tan(60° + θ)·cot(60° + θ) = 1. Hence LHS = 1/1 = 1 = RHS.
